modules.title: AI Foundations
modules.description: Learn ai foundations through focused explanations and runnable examples.

topics.title: AI, Machine Learning, Deep Learning, and Generative AI
topics.description: AI is the broad field; machine learning learns patterns from data; deep learning uses multilayer neural networks; generative AI produces new content. These categories overlap, but they are not interchangeable.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: AI is the broad field; machine learning learns patterns from data; deep learning uses multilayer neural networks; generative AI produces new content. These categories overlap, but they are not interchangeable. A chatbot is an application, while an LLM is a model used by that application.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: A useful hierarchy is AI → machine learning → deep learning, with generative AI describing systems that generate content rather than a strict child category of every deep-learning system. Machine learning can solve classification or regression without generating anything. Deep learning can perform recognition or prediction. Generative models learn distributions or representations that allow them to produce new sequences, images, audio, or other artifacts. In production, the distinction matters because the model is only one component: application code still handles identity, authorization, data access, business rules, validation, observability, and recovery.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: Consider an employee-support application. A deterministic rule can verify whether an employee may access a document; an ML classifier can route the request; an LLM can draft an explanation; retrieval can provide current policy text. Each component solves a different part of the problem.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: Map a real feature into four layers: deterministic application logic, learned predictive model, generative model, and surrounding infrastructure. Explain why each layer exists and which layer is authoritative.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Think of AI as a toolbox, not a single technology. The further a component moves from explicit rules toward learned generation, the more the system needs evaluation, uncertainty handling, and runtime controls.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Be ready to distinguish AI, ML, deep learning, generative AI, foundation models, LLMs, and AI applications. A strong answer explains that a model's capability does not replace application-level authorization or validation.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Do not claim that every AI system learns, that every generative model is an LLM, or that a chatbot itself is the model. Do not put authoritative permissions or financial calculations under probabilistic generation.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content: Use deterministic logic for exact rules, supervised ML for learned predictions, and generative models when flexible content or language interaction creates value. Avoid a generative model when a small deterministic function solves the problem more reliably.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: A support platform can combine retrieval, an LLM, deterministic policy checks, logging, rate limits, and human escalation. The model drafts; trusted services decide what data may be exposed and which actions may execute.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Machine learning paradigms, neural networks, foundation models, LLMs, prompting, retrieval-augmented generation, evaluation, guardrails, and AI system architecture.

topics.shortDescription: AI is the broad field; machine learning learns patterns from data; deep learning uses multilayer neural networks; generative AI produces new content. These categories overlap, but they are not interchangeable.

topics.title: Evolution of AI Applications
topics.description: AI applications evolved from explicit rules toward statistical learning, deep learning, and foundation-model-based systems.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: AI applications evolved from explicit rules toward statistical learning, deep learning, and foundation-model-based systems. Newer approaches did not make deterministic software obsolete; they expanded the range of problems software can address.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: Rule systems are strongest when domain knowledge can be written explicitly. Statistical ML learns patterns from examples. Deep learning improved representation learning for complex inputs such as images, speech, and text. Foundation models generalize across many tasks and can be adapted at runtime. Each transition brought new capabilities and new failure modes, so technology selection should follow the problem rather than fashion.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: An invoice pipeline might use deterministic parsing for a known file format, ML for anomaly detection, and a generative model to explain an anomaly to an operator.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: For one business process, design a rule-only version first, then identify the exact step where learned behavior would add value.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: The historical progression is a shift in where knowledge lives: hand-written rules, learned parameters, and increasingly reusable pretrained representations.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Explain why AI history is not simply a linear replacement of rules by neural networks. Discuss data, compute, generalization, auditability, and failure modes.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Do not equate newer with better. A large model can be slower, more expensive, less predictable, and harder to validate than a small algorithm.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content: Choose the simplest technique that meets quality requirements. Escalate to ML or generative AI when explicit logic becomes brittle or the task genuinely requires learned or open-ended behavior.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Use deterministic workflows around probabilistic components: classify or generate where flexibility helps, but validate schema, permissions, amounts, and state transitions with ordinary software.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Expert systems, statistical learning, deep learning, foundation models, model selection, evaluation, and production architecture.

topics.shortDescription: AI applications evolved from explicit rules toward statistical learning, deep learning, and foundation-model-based systems.

topics.title: Rule-Based and Logic Systems
topics.description: A rule-based system represents domain knowledge explicitly as facts, conditions, and actions.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: A rule-based system represents domain knowledge explicitly as facts, conditions, and actions.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: A rule engine evaluates known facts against rules such as IF condition THEN action. This is attractive when policies are explicit, deterministic, explainable, and frequently audited. The weakness is combinatorial growth: as exceptions interact, rule sets become difficult to maintain. A hybrid design can let an AI model interpret ambiguous input while deterministic rules remain authoritative for policy.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: A refund service can check `verifiedCustomer`, `amount > 0`, and `amount <= policyLimit` before permitting an operation. The decision can be logged with the exact rules that fired.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: Write three rules for a support workflow and test normal, conflicting, missing-data, and boundary cases.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Rules are executable policy. Their value comes from predictable state transitions, not from sounding intelligent.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Discuss forward chaining, rule evaluation, explainability, and why business-critical constraints should not depend solely on model instructions.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Avoid contradictory rules without precedence, hidden side effects, and placing rapidly changing natural-language knowledge into hard-coded conditions.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content: Use rules for authorization, limits, validation, calculations, and deterministic workflows. Avoid them when the input is highly ambiguous or the rule space changes faster than it can be maintained.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: A customer-service assistant can interpret a request with an LLM, but a policy service determines whether the customer is eligible for a refund and records the decision.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Expert systems, decision tables, authorization, guardrails, deterministic systems, and hybrid AI architecture.

topics.shortDescription: A rule-based system represents domain knowledge explicitly as facts, conditions, and actions.

topics.title: Early Machine Learning
topics.description: Early machine learning moved part of software behavior from hand-written rules to parameters learned from examples or feedback.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Early machine learning moved part of software behavior from hand-written rules to parameters learned from examples or feedback.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: The fundamental change is that engineers specify an objective and learning procedure rather than enumerating every decision. The model can discover statistical relationships, but it can also learn irrelevant or biased correlations. Data collection, feature design, evaluation, and generalization therefore become software-engineering concerns.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: A message classifier can learn from labeled examples of normal and urgent messages instead of maintaining hundreds of keyword rules.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: Take a rule-based classifier and list which examples would be required to train an equivalent learned model.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Code defines how learning happens; data defines much of what behavior is learned.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Explain the difference between training a model and writing a deterministic rule, especially in terms of generalization and failure modes.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Do not assume more training examples automatically produce better behavior. Leakage, biased sampling, noisy labels, and target mismatch can dominate model quality.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content: Use learning when patterns are difficult to encode explicitly and enough representative data exists. Avoid it when a transparent rule solves the task reliably.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: An ML classifier can route support tickets, while a deterministic fallback handles malformed requests and a monitoring system tracks distribution drift.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Supervised learning, statistical ML, deep learning, data quality, evaluation, and model monitoring.

topics.shortDescription: Early machine learning moved part of software behavior from hand-written rules to parameters learned from examples or feedback.

topics.title: AI Winters and the Importance of Realistic Expectations
topics.description: AI winters are periods when expectations and investment fell after AI systems failed to meet ambitious promises. The engineering lesson is to validate value instead of assuming technology alone creates it.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: AI winters are periods when expectations and investment fell after AI systems failed to meet ambitious promises. The engineering lesson is to validate value instead of assuming technology alone creates it.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: AI projects fail for many reasons: unclear objectives, unrealistic evaluation, insufficient data, high operating cost, poor workflow integration, or unreliable outputs. A useful AI project begins with a measurable user problem and explicit quality, latency, cost, privacy, and recovery requirements.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: If a support assistant saves agents only five seconds per case but introduces frequent factual errors, the feature may have negative value despite impressive demos.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: Define success metrics for an AI feature before selecting a model.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: A model benchmark measures capability; a product metric measures usefulness. They are related but not identical.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Discuss why an excellent model can still produce a failed AI product.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Avoid demo-driven development, single-example evaluation, and ignoring operational cost or human review.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content: Use AI when it improves a measurable workflow. Avoid it when the task is already solved more cheaply and reliably by deterministic software.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Run an offline evaluation set, pilot with real users, monitor quality and cost, and maintain a fallback path before broad rollout.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Evaluation, model selection, cost economics, UX, observability, and production AI.

topics.shortDescription: AI winters are periods when expectations and investment fell after AI systems failed to meet ambitious promises. The engineering lesson is to validate value instead of assuming technology alone creates it.

topics.title: Expert Systems
topics.description: An expert system separates domain knowledge from an inference mechanism that applies rules to a current case.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: An expert system separates domain knowledge from an inference mechanism that applies rules to a current case.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: A classic architecture contains a knowledge base, working memory, inference engine, and interaction layer. The separation makes reasoning explicit and auditable. Modern hybrid systems preserve the same idea by combining probabilistic interpretation with deterministic policy and workflow services.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: A feature-access service can keep customer facts in working memory and apply explicit eligibility rules through an inference function.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: Separate facts from rules in a small decision problem, then identify where an inference engine would operate.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Facts describe the case; rules describe allowed reasoning; the engine determines which rules apply.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Explain why expert systems were useful and why rule maintenance becomes difficult at scale.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Do not treat a large rule table as equivalent to learned intelligence, and do not allow untrusted model output to become authoritative facts without validation.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content: Use expert-system patterns when rules are explicit and auditability matters.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: A lending workflow can use a model to extract information from documents while an authoritative policy engine determines eligibility.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Rule engines, decision tables, knowledge bases, guardrails, and hybrid systems.

topics.shortDescription: An expert system separates domain knowledge from an inference mechanism that applies rules to a current case.

topics.title: Big Data and Statistical Machine Learning
topics.description: Large datasets made statistical learning useful at scales where manual rules or small samples were insufficient, but data volume alone does not guarantee better models.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Large datasets made statistical learning useful at scales where manual rules or small samples were insufficient, but data volume alone does not guarantee better models.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: Statistical ML depends on representative data, meaningful targets, suitable features or representations, and honest evaluation. Distributed storage and compute can make training practical for large datasets, but duplicated records, leakage, biased sampling, and label errors can make a huge dataset misleading.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: A machine-failure model may learn from temperature, vibration, and maintenance history. If records from the future leak into training, the offline score can look excellent while production performance collapses.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: Audit a hypothetical dataset for leakage, duplicates, missing labels, and distribution mismatch before training.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: The model learns from the evidence you provide, not from the business meaning you intended.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Explain why representative data and leakage prevention matter more than raw dataset size.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Confusing correlation with causation, random-splitting time-dependent data, and ignoring class imbalance.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content: Use statistical learning when measurable patterns exist and representative data is available.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Build a reproducible data pipeline, version training data, validate schemas, evaluate on realistic holdouts, and monitor drift after deployment.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Supervised learning, evaluation, feature engineering, data leakage, drift, and MLOps.

topics.shortDescription: Large datasets made statistical learning useful at scales where manual rules or small samples were insufficient, but data volume alone does not guarantee better models.

topics.title: Deep Learning
topics.description: Deep learning uses multilayer neural networks to learn representations and transformations from data.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Deep learning uses multilayer neural networks to learn representations and transformations from data.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: A neural network applies parameterized transformations, nonlinearities, and learned weights. During training, a loss function measures error and optimization adjusts parameters, typically through gradients. Depth allows representations to be composed, but performance depends on architecture, data, optimization, regularization, and compute.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: An image model may learn low-level visual patterns in early layers and combine them into increasingly task-specific representations in later layers.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: Draw a three-layer network and label input, parameters, activations, loss, and gradient flow.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Training is an optimization loop: predict → measure loss → compute gradients → update parameters → repeat.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Explain forward pass, loss, backpropagation, gradient descent, overfitting, and why deep learning needs substantial data/compute in many applications.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Do not describe deep learning as simply 'many layers' without discussing learned parameters and optimization. Do not assume training accuracy proves generalization.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content: Use deep learning for complex high-dimensional patterns such as vision, speech, and language. Avoid it for trivial deterministic logic.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Use versioned training data and model artifacts, reproducible training, accelerator-aware serving, latency monitoring, and rollback capability.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Neural networks, optimization, embeddings, Transformers, regularization, and model serving.

topics.shortDescription: Deep learning uses multilayer neural networks to learn representations and transformations from data.

topics.title: Foundation Models
topics.description: A foundation model is broadly trained so its learned capabilities can be adapted to many downstream tasks.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: A foundation model is broadly trained so its learned capabilities can be adapted to many downstream tasks.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: Foundation models shift effort from training a separate model for every task toward reusing a broadly pretrained model. Adaptation can happen through prompting, retrieval, tool use, fine-tuning, or other techniques. The model remains a component; application-specific permissions, context, evaluation, and business logic live around it.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: One foundation model can support summarization, coding assistance, document analysis, and support chat when each application supplies different instructions and context.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: For one product, list which requirements belong in the base model and which belong in application logic.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Think of a foundation model as a general capability layer; runtime context turns that capability into a task-specific system.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Define foundation model and distinguish pretraining from downstream adaptation.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Assuming broad pretraining means current knowledge, domain correctness, or guaranteed factuality.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content: Use foundation models when multiple tasks benefit from shared general capability and the adaptation cost is acceptable.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Version prompts, retrieval indexes, model identifiers, evaluation sets, and application policies independently so each can change safely.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Pretraining, LLMs, prompting, fine-tuning, embeddings, RAG, and model selection.

topics.shortDescription: A foundation model is broadly trained so its learned capabilities can be adapted to many downstream tasks.

topics.title: Large Language Models
topics.description: An LLM generates language by modeling relationships among tokens and producing a probability distribution over possible continuations.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: An LLM generates language by modeling relationships among tokens and producing a probability distribution over possible continuations.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: During generation, the model processes the supplied context and produces scores for candidate next tokens. The output is generated from learned parameters rather than retrieved from a guaranteed factual database. This explains both fluency and the possibility of unsupported statements. Reliability therefore comes from the full system, including retrieval, validation, constrained tools, and evaluation.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: If the model assigns probabilities to `approved`, `pending`, and `rejected`, decoding chooses one according to the selected strategy and then the process repeats with the new token.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: Trace three generation steps and distinguish model probabilities from the final text returned to a user.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: LLM generation is an iterative probabilistic loop over tokens, not a single lookup operation.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Explain next-token prediction, context, parameters, decoding, and why fluent output is not proof of truth.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Calling an LLM a database, assuming it always retrieves facts, or treating temperature as a factuality control.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content: Use LLMs for language-heavy tasks with tolerance for probabilistic output and appropriate validation.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Add retrieval for current facts, structured output validation, rate limits, tracing, content controls, and human escalation for high-impact cases.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Tokenization, Transformers, attention, decoding, prompting, RAG, and hallucination.

topics.shortDescription: An LLM generates language by modeling relationships among tokens and producing a probability distribution over possible continuations.

topics.title: GPT and Pretraining
topics.description: GPT refers to generative pretrained Transformer-based language-model families. Pretraining builds broad statistical capability before application-specific adaptation.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: GPT refers to generative pretrained Transformer-based language-model families. Pretraining builds broad statistical capability before application-specific adaptation.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: Pretraining learns parameters from large-scale data using an objective defined by the training procedure. Later stages can improve instruction following or specialize behavior. Runtime prompts and retrieved context are separate from what was learned during pretraining. This distinction is important because application data that is current today may not be part of the model's pretrained parameters.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: A support application can provide a base instruction plus current product documentation at runtime instead of assuming the model's pretrained knowledge contains the latest policy.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: Separate a system's pretrained capability, runtime prompt, retrieved context, and tool results on an architecture diagram.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Pretraining creates reusable capability; runtime context supplies the information needed for a particular request.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Explain what pretraining means and why runtime context is not the same as changing model parameters.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Do not imply that every GPT model has identical architecture, training data, context limits, or capabilities.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content: Use pretrained models when broad language capability is valuable; use adaptation techniques when general behavior is insufficient.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Track model version and prompt version separately, and evaluate each model upgrade because behavior can change even when application code does not.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Foundation models, Transformers, self-supervised learning, tokenization, fine-tuning, and evaluation.

topics.shortDescription: GPT refers to generative pretrained Transformer-based language-model families. Pretraining builds broad statistical capability before application-specific adaptation.

topics.title: Supervised Learning
topics.description: Supervised learning learns a mapping from inputs to known target labels or values.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Supervised learning learns a mapping from inputs to known target labels or values.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: Training examples contain features and a target. Classification predicts categories; regression predicts continuous values. The central engineering concern is generalization: evaluation must use data that represents unseen production cases. Splitting strategy depends on the data-generating process; time-dependent problems often require chronological validation rather than random shuffling.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: A support-routing model can learn from historical ticket text paired with the correct queue. A separate evaluation set measures performance on tickets not used for fitting.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: Given a dataset, identify input features, target, train/validation/test strategy, and an appropriate metric.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: The model is learning a rule from examples; the test set asks whether that learned rule transfers beyond the examples it saw.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Distinguish classification and regression, training and evaluation, overfitting and underfitting, and data leakage.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Using the test set repeatedly for tuning, leaking target information into features, and optimizing a metric that does not reflect business cost.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content: Use supervised learning when reliable labels or targets exist and prediction quality can be measured.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Monitor prediction distributions, error rates, delayed ground truth, drift, and performance by important segments.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Loss functions, evaluation metrics, cross-validation, overfitting, leakage, and model monitoring.

topics.shortDescription: Supervised learning learns a mapping from inputs to known target labels or values.

topics.title: Unsupervised Learning
topics.description: Unsupervised learning searches for structure in data without predefined target labels.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Unsupervised learning searches for structure in data without predefined target labels.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: Clustering, dimensionality reduction, and representation learning are common examples. Because there is no single supplied correct answer, evaluation often combines mathematical measures, visualization, stability, and domain usefulness. A discovered cluster is not automatically a meaningful business segment.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: Customer vectors can be grouped into low- and high-activity regions, but the resulting groups must be checked for stability and business meaning.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: Cluster a small dataset conceptually, then ask whether the clusters remain meaningful after changing scale or distance assumptions.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Unsupervised learning discovers structure under an objective; it does not discover objective business truth automatically.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Explain clustering, why scaling matters, and why evaluation is harder without labels.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Treating arbitrary clusters as facts, ignoring feature scaling, and selecting a cluster count without a reason.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content: Use it for exploration, segmentation, anomaly analysis, or representation discovery. Avoid it when the real task has a well-defined target that supervised learning can model.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Version preprocessing and clustering parameters, monitor population shifts, and validate that segments remain useful over time.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Clustering, dimensionality reduction, embeddings, anomaly detection, and evaluation.

topics.shortDescription: Unsupervised learning searches for structure in data without predefined target labels.

topics.title: Semi-Supervised Learning
topics.description: Semi-supervised learning combines a smaller labeled dataset with a larger unlabeled dataset.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Semi-supervised learning combines a smaller labeled dataset with a larger unlabeled dataset.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: The labeled portion provides explicit task information while unlabeled examples can contribute information about input structure, depending on the method's assumptions. The approach is useful when labels are expensive but raw data is plentiful. Unlabeled data must still be representative; adding more unrelated data can hurt rather than help.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: A defect-detection project may have 2,000 manually labeled images and 200,000 unlabeled factory images. A semi-supervised method can use both while keeping a clean labeled evaluation set.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: Design a data split that prevents unlabeled production data from accidentally contaminating a benchmark.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Labels tell the model what task matters; unlabeled data can tell it what the input population looks like.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Explain why semi-supervised learning is useful and what assumptions make it succeed or fail.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Treating pseudo-labels as ground truth, allowing evaluation examples into training, and ignoring population mismatch.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content: Use it when high-quality labels are expensive and representative unlabeled data is abundant.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Continuously sample uncertain predictions for human labeling and keep a protected evaluation set that is never used for training.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Supervised learning, self-supervised learning, pseudo-labeling, active learning, and evaluation.

topics.shortDescription: Semi-supervised learning combines a smaller labeled dataset with a larger unlabeled dataset.

topics.title: Reinforcement Learning
topics.description: Reinforcement learning learns through interaction with an environment using states, actions, rewards, and policies.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Reinforcement learning learns through interaction with an environment using states, actions, rewards, and policies.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: An agent observes a state, chooses an action, receives a reward, and transitions to another state. The objective concerns cumulative future reward, so an action that looks bad immediately can still be useful later. Reward design is critical because an agent can optimize a proxy objective while violating the real business intent.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: A warehouse robot may receive positive reward for reaching a destination efficiently and penalties for collisions or unnecessary movement.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: Define the state, action space, reward, and failure condition for a simple sequential problem.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: RL is about consequences over time, not merely matching an input to a known label.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Explain policy, reward, exploration versus exploitation, and why reward specification can cause unintended behavior.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Poor reward shaping, unsafe exploration, sparse feedback, and evaluating only short-term reward.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content: Use RL for sequential decisions where actions affect future states and meaningful feedback exists. Avoid it when a supervised or deterministic solution is sufficient.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Constrain actions with hard safety checks, simulate before deployment, monitor reward and real-world outcomes, and keep a safe fallback.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Markov decision processes, policies, value functions, exploration, simulation, and control.

topics.shortDescription: Reinforcement learning learns through interaction with an environment using states, actions, rewards, and policies.

topics.title: Self-Supervised Learning
topics.description: Self-supervised learning creates training targets from the data itself, allowing models to learn from large collections without manual labels for every example.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Self-supervised learning creates training targets from the data itself, allowing models to learn from large collections without manual labels for every example.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: Language models can be trained by predicting hidden or subsequent tokens. Vision systems can use transformations or masked portions of inputs. The key point is that the target is generated from the input data by the training procedure. The objective strongly influences which representations the model learns.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: Given `machine learning models`, a next-token objective can use `machine learning` as context and `models` as the target.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: Create three self-supervised training examples from a paragraph and identify the automatically generated target.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Self-supervision turns raw data into its own training signal.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Differentiate self-supervised, supervised, and unsupervised learning.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Calling self-supervised learning label-free without explaining that a training target still exists; confusing the pretraining objective with downstream evaluation.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content: Use it when large quantities of raw data exist and useful predictive or reconstruction objectives can be defined.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Filter and deduplicate training data, track data provenance, and evaluate whether the pretraining objective transfers to downstream tasks.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Pretraining, language modeling, embeddings, foundation models, and representation learning.

topics.shortDescription: Self-supervised learning creates training targets from the data itself, allowing models to learn from large collections without manual labels for every example.

topics.title: LLM Input Pipeline
topics.description: A simplified LLM request path is text or other input → token IDs → vector representations → Transformer computation → output scores → decoding.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: A simplified LLM request path is text or other input → token IDs → vector representations → Transformer computation → output scores → decoding.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: Tokenization converts input into vocabulary units. Embeddings represent tokens as vectors. Transformer blocks repeatedly transform these representations using attention and feed-forward computation, with residual and normalization mechanisms in practical architectures. The final representation is converted into logits or probabilities for possible next tokens, and a decoding strategy selects output tokens.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: For a short request, draw `text → [token IDs] → [vectors] → attention blocks → logits → selected token`, then append the selected token and repeat.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: Trace where context length, latency, and token usage enter this pipeline.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Every generated token requires another pass through the model's generation process; the growing sequence becomes part of the next context.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Explain tokenization, embeddings, attention, logits, and decoding in the correct order.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Saying the model directly 'looks up the answer' or confusing embeddings with final generated text.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content: Use this pipeline as the core mental model when reasoning about LLM latency, context limits, and generation.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Track token counts, request latency, model version, failures, and truncation behavior at the API boundary.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Tokenization, embeddings, Transformers, attention, logits, decoding, and context windows.

topics.shortDescription: A simplified LLM request path is text or other input → token IDs → vector representations → Transformer computation → output scores → decoding.

topics.title: Tokenization
topics.description: Tokenization maps raw input into discrete units that a particular model vocabulary can represent.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Tokenization maps raw input into discrete units that a particular model vocabulary can represent.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: A token may correspond to a whole word, subword fragment, punctuation mark, whitespace-related unit, or another vocabulary item. Token boundaries depend on the tokenizer, so character count and token count are not interchangeable. Tokenization affects context usage and, for many hosted services, cost and latency.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: The string `unhappiness` may be represented as several subword units depending on the tokenizer. A production application should measure with the actual tokenizer rather than a rough word-count heuristic.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: Compare short English, code, numbers, and multilingual text and observe why simple character-to-token ratios are unreliable.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: The model does not receive your text as characters; it receives token IDs defined by its tokenizer.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Explain why token count differs from word count and why tokenizer choice matters.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Hard-coding a universal tokens-per-word rule, ignoring truncation, and counting tokens with a different tokenizer than the deployed model.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content: Measure tokens when budgeting context, cost, latency, or request limits.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Budget input and output tokens, truncate or summarize safely, and record actual usage for cost analysis.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Embeddings, context windows, prompting, cost economics, batching, and model APIs.

topics.shortDescription: Tokenization maps raw input into discrete units that a particular model vocabulary can represent.

modules.description: Learn llm internals through focused explanations and runnable examples.

topics.title: Embeddings
topics.description: An embedding represents an item such as a token, sentence, document, product, or image as a vector in a learned or engineered space.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: An embedding represents an item such as a token, sentence, document, product, or image as a vector in a learned or engineered space.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: The useful property is that relationships can be represented geometrically. Similarity can be estimated with measures such as cosine similarity or distance, but the result depends on the embedding model and the data distribution. An embedding dimension is not normally a single human-interpretable concept; information is distributed across dimensions.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: Suppose support documents are embedded into vectors. A query embedding can be compared against document vectors to retrieve semantically related material even when the wording differs.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: Explain why `refund my money` can be close to `request a reimbursement` even when the strings share few words.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Embeddings turn discrete or complex objects into coordinates that make certain relationships easier to compute.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Explain embeddings, vector similarity, cosine similarity, and why embedding quality affects retrieval.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Assuming nearest vector always means factual relevance, ignoring normalization/distance choice, or mixing incompatible embedding spaces.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content: Use embeddings for semantic retrieval, clustering, recommendation, similarity, or matching.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Version the embedding model, re-embed when changing models, store metadata with vectors, and evaluate retrieval quality with real queries.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Vector databases, semantic search, RAG, tokenization, similarity metrics, and clustering.

topics.shortDescription: An embedding represents an item such as a token, sentence, document, product, or image as a vector in a learned or engineered space.

topics.title: Contextual Meaning
topics.description: Language meaning often depends on surrounding context, so useful representations must incorporate information from neighboring tokens.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Language meaning often depends on surrounding context, so useful representations must incorporate information from neighboring tokens.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: The word `bank` can refer to a financial institution or a river edge. Contextual Transformer computation allows token representations to be influenced by other positions. This is why modern language systems can distinguish meanings that keyword matching alone cannot.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: Compare `She deposited the cheque at the bank` with `The hikers sat beside the river bank`. The surrounding words change the likely interpretation of `bank`.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: Find three ambiguous words and list the context signals needed to disambiguate them.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: A token's useful representation is contextual rather than a permanent dictionary definition.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Explain why contextual representations improve language understanding and how attention contributes.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Assuming one embedding vector always has one fixed meaning regardless of context.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content: Use contextual language models for ambiguity, references, semantic interpretation, and language-heavy tasks.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Provide sufficient but relevant context and evaluate ambiguous, adversarial, and domain-specific inputs.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Attention, Transformers, embeddings, tokenization, semantic search, and language modeling.

topics.shortDescription: Language meaning often depends on surrounding context, so useful representations must incorporate information from neighboring tokens.

topics.title: Transformer Layers and Self-Attention
topics.description: Self-attention lets each token compute how strongly information from other positions should influence its representation.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Self-attention lets each token compute how strongly information from other positions should influence its representation.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: Each position is projected into query, key, and value representations. Query-key compatibility produces attention scores; normalized weights determine how value vectors are combined. Practical Transformer blocks also contain multiple heads, feed-forward networks, residual connections, normalization, and positional information. Attention is powerful because it provides direct interactions between positions in the context.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: For `The server returned an error because it was unavailable`, attention can help the representation of `it` incorporate information from relevant earlier tokens. This is a conceptual illustration, not a guarantee of a single attention head performing a specific linguistic role.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: Draw a three-token sequence and label Q, K, V, attention scores, normalized weights, and weighted value sum.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Attention is a content-dependent routing mechanism: each position asks which other positions are useful right now.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Explain Q/K/V, softmax-normalized attention weights, multi-head attention, residual connections, and positional information.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Saying attention simply 'finds the most important word', assuming one head has one fixed semantic meaning, or omitting computational cost.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content: Use the Transformer mental model when explaining contextualization, long-range dependencies, and LLM architecture.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Model size and sequence length affect latency and compute. Monitor context sizes and choose architectures/models appropriate to the workload.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Transformers, embeddings, positional encoding, feed-forward networks, normalization, and decoding.

topics.shortDescription: Self-attention lets each token compute how strongly information from other positions should influence its representation.

topics.title: Next-Token Prediction and Decoding
topics.description: At generation time, a language model produces scores or probabilities for possible next tokens, and a decoding strategy turns that distribution into output.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: At generation time, a language model produces scores or probabilities for possible next tokens, and a decoding strategy turns that distribution into output.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: Greedy decoding selects the highest-probability token. Sampling can introduce variation by drawing from a probability distribution, often after transformations such as temperature or top-p filtering. These controls affect diversity and reproducibility but do not independently guarantee factual correctness.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: If probabilities are `resolved=.58`, `pending=.27`, `failed=.15`, greedy decoding selects `resolved`; a sampling strategy may choose another token depending on its configured distribution.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: Compare greedy selection with sampling conceptually and explain what changes when the probability distribution is flatter.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Generation is a repeated decision loop: produce distribution → choose token → append token → repeat until a stopping condition.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Explain logits, probabilities, greedy decoding, sampling, temperature, top-p, and why decoding does not fix knowledge errors.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Claiming temperature makes a model more truthful, or that the highest-probability token is always the correct answer.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content: Use conservative decoding for structured/repeatable tasks and more varied sampling when diversity is useful.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Define stopping behavior, maximum output length, structured-output validation, and evaluation across representative prompts.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: LLMs, softmax, logits, tokenization, structured generation, and evaluation.

topics.shortDescription: At generation time, a language model produces scores or probabilities for possible next tokens, and a decoding strategy turns that distribution into output.

modules.title: Generation and Application Design
modules.description: Learn generation and application design through focused explanations and runnable examples.

topics.title: What Makes Generative AI Different
topics.description: Generative AI produces open-ended outputs, so the software contract must handle uncertainty, variation, and user review.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Generative AI produces open-ended outputs, so the software contract must handle uncertainty, variation, and user review.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: A traditional program may return a fixed class or exact calculation. A generative system can produce many plausible outputs for the same intent. That creates new requirements for evaluation, output validation, UX, safety, source grounding, and recovery. The system should be designed around acceptable behavior rather than assuming a single exact string.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: A tax calculator should return an authoritative number from deterministic rules, while a generative assistant can explain the result in natural language after the number has been computed.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: Take a deterministic feature and a generative feature and compare their input/output contracts.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Generative output is a distribution of possibilities, so downstream software must define what counts as acceptable.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Explain how probabilistic output changes testing, UX, monitoring, and system design.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Using exact string assertions for inherently variable output, or letting generated text directly execute sensitive actions.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content: Use generation for drafting, transformation, summarization, and flexible interaction; avoid it for exact calculations or authoritative state changes.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Separate generation from execution. Validate structured fields and require confirmation for consequential actions.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Probabilistic systems, prompting, evaluation, guardrails, UX, and tool calling.

topics.shortDescription: Generative AI produces open-ended outputs, so the software contract must handle uncertainty, variation, and user review.

topics.title: Deterministic versus Probabilistic Systems
topics.description: Deterministic systems aim for predictable results from the same state; probabilistic systems may produce different valid outputs.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Deterministic systems aim for predictable results from the same state; probabilistic systems may produce different valid outputs.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: Deterministic code is ideal for permissions, calculations, state transitions, and validation. Probabilistic models are useful when multiple outputs can be acceptable and the task depends on ambiguous language or patterns. Production systems often combine both: AI interprets or proposes, trusted code validates and executes.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: A model can interpret `move 700 dollars to savings`, but the banking service should verify balance, authorization, limits, and transaction state before execution.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: Mark every component of an AI workflow as deterministic, probabilistic, or a boundary between the two.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Treat probabilistic output as an untrusted proposal until the system has verified whatever matters for the action.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Explain where deterministic boundaries should exist in an AI-enabled transaction workflow.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Using prompts as authorization, trusting generated amounts, and failing to define a fallback.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content: Combine both approaches whenever AI adds interpretation but exact business outcomes are required.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Use schemas, authorization checks, idempotency, transactional services, audit logs, and human confirmation where appropriate.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Guardrails, tool use, function calling, validation, authorization, and AI architecture.

topics.shortDescription: Deterministic systems aim for predictable results from the same state; probabilistic systems may produce different valid outputs.

topics.title: Prompt Design
topics.description: A production prompt communicates task, context, constraints, and output expectations to a generative model.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: A production prompt communicates task, context, constraints, and output expectations to a generative model.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: Prompts should be treated as versioned application assets. A useful prompt separates trusted instructions from untrusted user content, supplies only relevant context, and specifies output requirements appropriate to the task. Prompt quality should be evaluated across a representative dataset rather than judged from one successful response.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: A support classifier can specify allowed labels and require exactly one label, while placing the customer message in a clearly delimited variable.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: Rewrite a vague prompt by adding task, context, constraints, output format, and failure behavior.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Prompting is interface design for a probabilistic component, not magic wording.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Discuss zero-shot/few-shot prompting, structured outputs, prompt injection, and evaluation.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Overlong prompts, contradictory instructions, leaking secrets into context, and assuming prompt instructions are security controls.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content: Use explicit templates, examples, schemas, and relevant context when they improve measurable performance.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Version prompts, run regression evaluations, log safe metadata, and test adversarial and ambiguous inputs before deployment.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: RAG, prompt injection, structured outputs, evaluation, context windows, and guardrails.

topics.shortDescription: A production prompt communicates task, context, constraints, and output expectations to a generative model.

topics.title: Multimodal AI
topics.description: Multimodal AI combines multiple input or output modalities such as text, images, audio, and video.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Multimodal AI combines multiple input or output modalities such as text, images, audio, and video.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: A multimodal application may combine a photograph with a text description, or use audio and text together. Each modality has its own preprocessing and error modes. The important engineering principle is to identify which information is authoritative and validate high-impact extracted facts.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: A device-support workflow can accept a photo of a damaged connector plus a written symptom. The model can draft troubleshooting steps, but a technician or deterministic diagnostic system may still verify critical findings.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: Design a multimodal request and list the failure modes for each modality.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Adding a modality adds information but also adds another uncertainty surface.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Explain multimodal input, fusion at a high level, and why multimodal output still needs validation.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Assuming image understanding is perfect, ignoring OCR/speech errors, and using generated descriptions as authoritative evidence.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content: Use multimodal systems when combining modalities materially improves task performance.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Store modality provenance, validate extracted facts, control file sizes/types, and monitor errors separately by modality.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Vision models, speech recognition, embeddings, context, UX, and safety.

topics.shortDescription: Multimodal AI combines multiple input or output modalities such as text, images, audio, and video.

modules.title: Safety and Reliability
modules.description: Learn safety and reliability through focused explanations and runnable examples.

topics.title: User Experience for Generative Applications
topics.description: Generative UX should preserve user control because output can be useful, uncertain, variable, or wrong.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Generative UX should preserve user control because output can be useful, uncertain, variable, or wrong.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: Good interfaces let users inspect, edit, regenerate, reject, and recover from generated content. For actions with side effects, preview and confirmation are often more appropriate than silent execution. Source visibility can improve trust when the system is grounded in retrieved information.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: An email assistant can show a draft with edit and regenerate controls, while sending the message remains a user-confirmed action.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: Sketch the happy path and failure/recovery path for an AI writing feature.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: The interface is part of the reliability system: it determines whether users can catch and recover from model errors.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Discuss human-in-the-loop UX, confirmation, source attribution, and graceful failure.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Anthropomorphic claims, hiding uncertainty, auto-executing consequential actions, and making regeneration the only recovery option.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content: Use generative UI where flexibility helps; keep deterministic workflows for simple, repetitive operations.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Measure task completion, edit rate, rejection rate, latency, user corrections, and safety incidents—not just model response quality.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Human-in-the-loop, guardrails, hallucination, evaluation, accessibility, and workflow design.

topics.shortDescription: Generative UX should preserve user control because output can be useful, uncertain, variable, or wrong.

topics.title: Guardrails
topics.description: Guardrails are layered controls that reduce the probability or impact of unsafe, incorrect, unauthorized, or unwanted AI behavior.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Guardrails are layered controls that reduce the probability or impact of unsafe, incorrect, unauthorized, or unwanted AI behavior.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: Effective guardrails operate at multiple layers: identity and authorization, input validation, context selection, prompt structure, tool permissions, output validation, rate limiting, monitoring, and human review. A prompt can guide behavior but is not a security boundary. Authoritative policies belong in trusted application code.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: Before a model can trigger a refund tool, the backend should authenticate the user, verify authorization, validate the amount, enforce business limits, and log the operation.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: Threat-model an AI agent and place at least one control before input, during model/tool interaction, and after output.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Security comes from constrained capabilities and trusted enforcement, not from asking the model to behave.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Explain prompt injection, least privilege, output validation, and why model instructions cannot replace authorization.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Relying on system prompts alone, giving tools excessive permissions, and validating only the model's natural-language response.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content: Use layered guardrails whenever model output can affect users, data, tools, or external systems.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Implement least-privilege credentials, allowlisted tools, parameter validation, rate limits, audit logs, and kill switches.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Prompt injection, authorization, tool calling, privacy, monitoring, and secure architecture.

topics.shortDescription: Guardrails are layered controls that reduce the probability or impact of unsafe, incorrect, unauthorized, or unwanted AI behavior.

topics.title: Hallucination and Reliability
topics.description: Hallucination describes generated content that is unsupported, incorrect, or presented with unjustified confidence.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Hallucination describes generated content that is unsupported, incorrect, or presented with unjustified confidence.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: The risk varies by task. Creative drafting can tolerate some uncertainty; account management, finance, legal, security, and other high-impact workflows require stronger controls. Mitigation is a system-design problem: retrieve authoritative information, constrain actions, validate outputs, cite evidence where appropriate, and escalate when confidence or evidence is insufficient.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: A warranty assistant should retrieve the current warranty policy and cite the relevant passage rather than relying only on model memory.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: For five sample questions, decide whether the system needs retrieval, deterministic validation, human review, or none of these.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Reliability is a property of the complete pipeline, not a single model score.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Explain why hallucinations happen at a high level and how RAG, validation, structured outputs, and human review reduce risk.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Treating confidence-like wording as factual confidence, adding irrelevant retrieval, and assuming citations automatically make an answer correct.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content: Use stronger grounding and verification as the cost of error increases.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Track unsupported-answer rate, citation correctness, retrieval recall, escalation rate, and user corrections.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: RAG, evaluation, guardrails, source attribution, uncertainty, and observability.

topics.shortDescription: Hallucination describes generated content that is unsupported, incorrect, or presented with unjustified confidence.

paths.description: Production architecture, economics, privacy, engineering, model selection, and end-to-end AI system design.

modules.title: Model Operations
modules.description: Learn model operations through focused explanations and runnable examples.

topics.title: Hosted versus Self-Hosted Models
topics.description: Hosted models trade infrastructure responsibility for provider dependency; self-hosted models trade that dependency for greater operational control.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Hosted models trade infrastructure responsibility for provider dependency; self-hosted models trade that dependency for greater operational control.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: Hosted APIs can reduce serving complexity and provide rapid access to advanced capabilities, but introduce network dependency, provider pricing, limits, availability considerations, and data-handling requirements. Self-hosting gives more control over deployment and data paths but requires capacity planning, model serving, scaling, upgrades, monitoring, and hardware management.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: A prototype may use a hosted API for speed, while a regulated workload may investigate self-hosting if its privacy and operational requirements justify the additional complexity.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: Score both approaches against privacy, latency, cost, customization, availability, and engineering capacity.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: The decision moves operational responsibility between your team and the provider; it does not remove that responsibility.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Compare latency, cost, privacy, scalability, vendor lock-in, and operational burden.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Comparing only API price against hardware price, ignoring engineering labor, or assuming self-hosting automatically means better privacy.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content: Choose hosted for speed and reduced ops; consider self-hosting when control, customization, or specific deployment constraints justify it.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Run a benchmark using realistic traffic and include model serving, observability, failover, data governance, and capacity costs.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Model selection, cost economics, privacy, inference serving, scaling, and architecture.

topics.shortDescription: Hosted models trade infrastructure responsibility for provider dependency; self-hosted models trade that dependency for greater operational control.

topics.title: Cost and Token Economics
topics.description: AI cost is influenced by model choice, input/output volume, request frequency, and architecture; token usage is one important cost driver for many hosted LLM services.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: AI cost is influenced by model choice, input/output volume, request frequency, and architecture; token usage is one important cost driver for many hosted LLM services.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: Long prompts, repeated history, unnecessary retrieved documents, and verbose outputs can increase cost and latency. Optimization should preserve useful context rather than blindly minimizing tokens. Common techniques include retrieval filtering, summarization, caching safe results, smaller models for simple tasks, batching where supported, and output constraints. Actual pricing is provider- and model-specific and should be measured from current provider documentation.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: If a workflow sends the same 20-page policy on every request, retrieving only the relevant sections can reduce input volume while improving focus.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: Estimate cost per task from requests per user, average input/output usage, model price, and traffic volume.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: The real unit of economics is often a completed workflow, not a single model call.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Explain token-based cost, model routing, caching, and why a cheaper model can increase total cost if it causes retries or poor outcomes.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Using stale pricing assumptions, ignoring retries, and optimizing token count without measuring quality.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content: Optimize aggressively for high-volume workflows; preserve stronger models when their quality materially improves business outcomes.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Track cost per request, cost per successful task, token distribution, retry rate, cache hit rate, and model mix.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Tokenization, model routing, caching, latency, batching, and unit economics.

topics.shortDescription: AI cost is influenced by model choice, input/output volume, request frequency, and architecture; token usage is one important cost driver for many hosted LLM services.

topics.title: Privacy and Intellectual Property
topics.description: AI systems can process sensitive information and copyrighted or licensed material, so data governance must be designed into the pipeline.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: AI systems can process sensitive information and copyrighted or licensed material, so data governance must be designed into the pipeline.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: Privacy and intellectual-property questions depend on the data, jurisdiction, contracts, provider terms, and intended use. Engineering controls include data minimization, access control, retention limits, redaction where appropriate, encryption, provenance tracking, and clear rules about what data may enter prompts, retrieval indexes, logs, or training pipelines. Legal review may be required for high-risk use cases.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: A support system can redact unnecessary personal identifiers before sending a request to an external model and restrict retrieval to documents the authenticated user is allowed to access.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: Trace a sensitive document from ingestion to retrieval, model request, logs, storage, and deletion, and identify every place data could leak.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Privacy is a data-flow property. Protecting the database is insufficient if the same data is copied into prompts, logs, caches, or third-party services.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Discuss data minimization, access control, retention, provenance, and why legal requirements vary by context.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Assuming a model provider's generic policy answers every legal question, logging raw prompts indefinitely, or retrieving documents without user-level authorization.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content: Apply stricter controls whenever personal, confidential, proprietary, or regulated data is involved.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Use a documented data classification policy, least-privilege retrieval, configurable retention, audit logs, and provider contracts reviewed by the appropriate teams.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Security, RAG authorization, governance, data lineage, compliance, and threat modeling.

topics.shortDescription: AI systems can process sensitive information and copyrighted or licensed material, so data governance must be designed into the pipeline.

topics.title: When Generative AI Is a Good Fit
topics.description: Generative AI is a good fit when flexible language or content generation creates measurable value and the system can tolerate or control probabilistic output.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Generative AI is a good fit when flexible language or content generation creates measurable value and the system can tolerate or control probabilistic output.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: Strong candidates include drafting, summarization, transformation, conversational interfaces, code assistance, and synthesis of unstructured information. Weak candidates include exact calculations, hard authorization decisions, and simple deterministic transformations. The right choice depends on error cost, data availability, user workflow, latency, cost, and validation options.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: Generating a first draft of a support response is a strong fit; calculating an invoice total should remain deterministic.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: Evaluate ten candidate product features and classify each as deterministic, ML, generative, or hybrid.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: The question is not 'Can a model do this?' but 'Does generation improve the complete workflow enough to justify its uncertainty and cost?'

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Give a framework for deciding whether to use generative AI and discuss alternatives.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Starting from a model and searching for a problem, ignoring simpler solutions, and measuring demo quality instead of task outcomes.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content: Prefer generation for high-variance language tasks; avoid it for exact, safety-critical, or easily automated logic unless tightly constrained.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Prototype against representative tasks, establish acceptance criteria, measure human correction, and keep a deterministic fallback where possible.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Model selection, evaluation, UX, cost economics, deterministic systems, and architecture.

topics.shortDescription: Generative AI is a good fit when flexible language or content generation creates measurable value and the system can tolerate or control probabilistic output.
