topics.title: AI-Enhanced Customer Service
topics.description: AI can improve customer service by helping agents or customers retrieve information, summarize cases, classify requests, and draft responses.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: AI can improve customer service by helping agents or customers retrieve information, summarize cases, classify requests, and draft responses.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: A robust support architecture separates retrieval and policy from generation. The model can interpret intent and draft language, while authorization controls which customer records are visible and trusted services execute account changes. Human escalation remains important for ambiguous or high-impact cases.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: A support assistant retrieves the customer's eligible product documentation and case history, drafts a response, cites the sources, and lets an agent approve before sending.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: Design the flow for authentication, retrieval, generation, review, and escalation.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: The assistant should reduce cognitive work without becoming an uncontrolled decision-maker.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Discuss RAG, access control, hallucination mitigation, agent assist, and evaluation metrics.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Cross-customer data leakage, unsupported policy claims, and auto-executing account changes.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content: Use AI for summarization, drafting, classification, search assistance, and repetitive agent workflows.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Measure resolution time, first-contact resolution, escalation accuracy, correction rate, groundedness, and customer satisfaction.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: RAG, guardrails, UX, embeddings, authorization, and observability.

topics.shortDescription: AI can improve customer service by helping agents or customers retrieve information, summarize cases, classify requests, and draft responses.

topics.title: Generative Writing Assistance
topics.description: Generative writing tools transform or create text while keeping a human or downstream process responsible for final acceptance.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Generative writing tools transform or create text while keeping a human or downstream process responsible for final acceptance.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: Useful operations include drafting, rewriting, summarizing, tone transformation, outlining, and extracting structured information. Quality should be evaluated for factual preservation, instruction following, style, and unintended changes. For professional content, source material and user edits remain important.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: A support agent can provide bullet points and ask for a concise customer response. The system can draft text while preserving named facts and leaving unsupported details out.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: Compare a generated rewrite against the source and mark factual changes separately from stylistic changes.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Writing assistance is a constrained transformation problem when source facts must survive unchanged.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Discuss prompt constraints, factual preservation, evaluation, and human review.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Inventing facts, changing numbers or names, and assuming polished language means correct content.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content: Use for drafting and transformation when a person can review the result; add stronger controls when text has legal or financial consequences.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Store source and generated versions separately, provide diff/review UI, and evaluate factual preservation on representative examples.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Prompt design, evaluation, UX, hallucination, structured outputs, and content governance.

topics.shortDescription: Generative writing tools transform or create text while keeping a human or downstream process responsible for final acceptance.

topics.title: Image Generation
topics.description: Image generation models produce images from learned representations conditioned on inputs such as text or reference images.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Image generation models produce images from learned representations conditioned on inputs such as text or reference images.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: Generative image systems can support concept exploration, marketing variations, mockups, and creative workflows. Output can vary and may contain visual or semantic errors. The engineering problem includes prompt conditioning, reference control, resolution, latency, moderation, provenance, and intellectual-property considerations.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: A product team can generate several packaging concepts from a textual brief, then have a designer select and refine the best direction.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: Define quality criteria for composition, text rendering, brand constraints, and prohibited content before evaluating generated images.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Image generation is a probabilistic synthesis process, not a guaranteed rendering of every instruction.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Discuss conditioning, variability, evaluation, safety, and why generated imagery needs review.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Assuming exact text or geometry will always render correctly, ignoring licensing/provenance questions, and using generated assets without review in high-stakes contexts.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content: Use for ideation and controlled creative production; use deterministic design tools when exact geometry or typography is mandatory.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Add moderation, brand review, provenance metadata where applicable, asset versioning, and human approval before publication.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Multimodal AI, diffusion-style generation, prompt design, safety, provenance, and UX.

topics.shortDescription: Image generation models produce images from learned representations conditioned on inputs such as text or reference images.

topics.title: AI Engineering
topics.description: AI engineering is the discipline of turning model capabilities into reliable software products through data, prompts, retrieval, tools, evaluation, security, and operations.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: AI engineering is the discipline of turning model capabilities into reliable software products through data, prompts, retrieval, tools, evaluation, security, and operations.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: The model is only one dependency. AI engineering covers input preparation, context construction, model invocation, structured outputs, tool integration, evaluation, observability, cost control, and failure handling. Unlike ordinary deterministic software, model behavior can change with model versions, prompts, data, and runtime context, so regression evaluation is essential.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: An enterprise assistant may contain authentication, document retrieval, prompt construction, LLM invocation, output parsing, tool authorization, logging, evaluation, and fallback paths.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: Draw an end-to-end AI feature and label every boundary where deterministic validation or monitoring is needed.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: AI engineering is systems engineering around a probabilistic component.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Explain evaluation, RAG, tool calling, prompt versioning, observability, cost, and security as one architecture.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Only tuning prompts, skipping evaluation, coupling business logic to model text, and lacking rollback/fallback mechanisms.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content: Use disciplined AI engineering practices for any production feature whose behavior depends on models.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Build versioned prompts, tests, eval datasets, tracing, model routing, guardrails, and deployment rollback into the lifecycle.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: MLOps, LLMOps, RAG, evaluation, security, model selection, and observability.

topics.shortDescription: AI engineering is the discipline of turning model capabilities into reliable software products through data, prompts, retrieval, tools, evaluation, security, and operations.

topics.title: Model Selection
topics.description: Model selection is choosing a model based on the application's quality, latency, cost, context, modality, privacy, and operational requirements.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Model selection is choosing a model based on the application's quality, latency, cost, context, modality, privacy, and operational requirements.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: A larger or newer model is not automatically the best choice. Evaluate candidate models on representative tasks, including failure cases. Consider input/output limits, tool or structured-output support, throughput, latency, cost, deployment constraints, and provider availability. Use the smallest model that meets the required quality when economics matter.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: A routing workflow might use a small classifier for intent detection and reserve a stronger LLM for difficult free-form requests.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: Create a scorecard for three candidate models using quality, latency, cost, and reliability weights.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Model choice is an optimization problem under constraints, not a popularity contest.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Explain benchmark versus task-specific evaluation and why production metrics matter.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Using public benchmarks as the only evidence, ignoring tail latency, and selecting a model before defining acceptance criteria.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content: Compare models whenever quality, cost, latency, or capability requirements are material.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Run offline evals, shadow traffic where appropriate, canary releases, and monitor quality/cost before changing the default model.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Cost economics, evaluation, model routing, latency, benchmarking, and deployment.

topics.shortDescription: Model selection is choosing a model based on the application's quality, latency, cost, context, modality, privacy, and operational requirements.

topics.title: Production Architecture
topics.description: Production AI architecture surrounds model inference with identity, data access, context construction, validation, observability, and recovery mechanisms.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Production AI architecture surrounds model inference with identity, data access, context construction, validation, observability, and recovery mechanisms.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: A typical request path may include API authentication, input validation, retrieval, prompt/context construction, model invocation, output parsing, tool authorization, response filtering, logging, and feedback collection. Stateful workflows may also need queues, caches, rate limits, retries, idempotency, and asynchronous processing.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: A support request can authenticate the user, retrieve authorized documents, generate an answer, validate structured fields, and return citations while recording trace metadata.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: Draw the architecture and identify where each failure can occur and how the system recovers.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Reliability emerges from boundaries around the model: every uncertain component needs an appropriate control.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Design an AI assistant with RAG, caching, rate limits, observability, authorization, and failure handling.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Single point of failure, unlimited context, unbounded retries, missing authorization on retrieval, and no model fallback.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content: Use layered architecture for production AI rather than direct browser-to-model calls.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Combine stateless APIs, secure retrieval, model gateway/routing, validation, tracing, quotas, queues where needed, and rollback.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: RAG, guardrails, AI engineering, scalability, caching, observability, and security.

topics.shortDescription: Production AI architecture surrounds model inference with identity, data access, context construction, validation, observability, and recovery mechanisms.

topics.title: Interview and Revision Master Section
topics.description: Strong AI interviews test whether you can explain concepts, make trade-offs, reason about failure modes, and design reliable systems—not merely define terms.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Strong AI interviews test whether you can explain concepts, make trade-offs, reason about failure modes, and design reliable systems—not merely define terms.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: A reusable answer structure is: define the concept, explain the mechanism, give a concrete example, state trade-offs, identify failure modes, and connect it to production. For system-design questions, establish requirements before selecting a model or architecture.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: For 'design a customer-support assistant,' discuss users and data first, then retrieval, model choice, authorization, guardrails, evaluation, latency, cost, and fallback.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: Answer an AI design question aloud using the sequence: requirements → architecture → model → data/context → safety → evaluation → operations.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Interview reasoning is about making assumptions explicit and defending them.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Prepare comparisons: supervised vs unsupervised, self-supervised vs supervised, RAG vs fine-tuning, hosted vs self-hosted, deterministic vs probabilistic, and small vs large models.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Giving vendor-specific claims without qualification, skipping requirements, confusing model capability with product reliability, and using buzzwords without mechanisms.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content: Use this framework whenever an interview asks 'why', 'how', 'which approach', or 'design a system'.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: A good interview answer should resemble a production review: requirements, trade-offs, failure handling, observability, and measurable success criteria.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: All preceding AI/ML/LLM concepts, system design, behavioral trade-offs, and evaluation.

topics.shortDescription: Strong AI interviews test whether you can explain concepts, make trade-offs, reason about failure modes, and design reliable systems—not merely define terms.

topics.title: Capstone Project — Safe AI Support Assistant
topics.description: A safe AI support assistant combines retrieval, generation, authorization, validation, observability, and human escalation into one end-to-end system.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: A safe AI support assistant combines retrieval, generation, authorization, validation, observability, and human escalation into one end-to-end system.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: The assistant should authenticate the user, retrieve only documents and records they are authorized to access, construct relevant context, invoke the model, validate the output, and present the answer with evidence when appropriate. It should not let generated text bypass business rules. High-impact actions should use constrained tools and explicit confirmation.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: A customer asks about warranty coverage. The system authenticates the customer, retrieves the current warranty policy and permitted case information, generates a concise answer with source references, and offers escalation if the evidence is insufficient.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: Implement the capstone in phases: deterministic mock retrieval → model integration → structured output → authorization → evaluation → monitoring → failure simulation.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: The model is the reasoning/generation component; the application remains the authority over identity, data access, state, and side effects.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Be prepared to defend the architecture, threat model, evaluation plan, cost model, and fallback strategy.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Prompt-only security, cross-user retrieval leakage, trusting unsupported answers, exposing raw internal documents, and auto-executing account changes.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content: Use the architecture as a reference implementation for learning production AI patterns. Avoid copying it unchanged into a real regulated system without domain-specific security and legal review.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Add authentication, authorization-aware retrieval, rate limiting, prompt-injection defenses, output validation, audit logging, evaluation datasets, human escalation, and operational dashboards.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: RAG, embeddings, guardrails, prompt injection, UX, model selection, production architecture, and AI engineering.

topics.shortDescription: A safe AI support assistant combines retrieval, generation, authorization, validation, observability, and human escalation into one end-to-end system.
